items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, HUMAN DIPLOMACY: FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
items.abstract: This article examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern diplomacy and explores the boundary between AI assistance and human diplomatic authority. It discusses how AI can support diplomatic work through public opinion analysis, translation, information processing, crisis monitoring, early-warning systems, and negotiation preparation. At the same time, the article considers significant risks, including bias, inaccurate outputs, misinformation, cybersecurity threats, privacy concerns, and cultural and contextual misunderstanding. Drawing on examples and evaluations from the U.S. Department of State, UNESCO, the OECD, and the U.S. Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy, the article argues that AI should strengthen rather than replace human decision-making. While AI can improve the speed and efficiency of analyzing information, political judgment, ethical responsibility, interpersonal understanding, and decisions involving significant human consequences should remain under human authority.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, the knowledge problem, and academic judgment: an Austrian perspective
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have renewed claims that university teaching and research can be largely automated. This article argues that such claims confuse information processing with judgment. Drawing on Hayek’s theory of dispersed and tacit knowledge, Huerta de Soto’s analysis of computation and entrepreneurial discovery, and the theory of judgment under Knightian uncertainty, it explains why greater computational capacity does not eliminate the knowledge problem. Contemporary AI can retrieve, recombine, and generate large volumes of context-sensitive information, while memory and retrieval mechanisms allow earlier interactions to shape later outputs. These capabilities expand the range of plausible explanations and possible courses of inquiry, but they do not provide a purpose-independent criterion for determining which interpretation is relevant, which assumptions are defensible, or which course of action should be pursued. The article applies this distinction to higher education. Artificial intelligence is likely to substitute for some standardized and information-intensive academic tasks, including routine content delivery, retrieval, and preliminary synthesis. At the same time, it increases the relative importance of judgment-intensive functions: diagnosing misunderstanding, selecting worthwhile research questions, evaluating methods and evidence, mentoring students, and assigning responsibility for scholarly claims. The argument is therefore not that every existing university practice will persist unchanged, but that artificial intelligence shifts the comparative advantage of professors and universities toward the cultivation, evaluation, and institutional coordination of judgment under uncertainty.

items.title: Availability of performance evidence of approved AI diagnostic software in pathology and hematology morphology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML)-based in vitro diagnostic software is increasingly authorized for clinical use in digital pathology and hematology morphology. However, it remains unclear how often performance evidence is publicly available. We performed a systematic landscape analysis identifying 77 CE-marked or FDA-authorized AI/ML-based IVD software devices from 29 manufacturers, including 68 digital pathology and 9 hematology morphology devices, identified through a multi-source search of FDA databases, EUDAMED, PubMed, Google Scholar, manufacturer portfolios, and clinical conference proceedings. Publicly available device-specific performance evidence was identified for 30 devices (39%), while 47 devices (61%) had no identified publicly available performance evidence. Evidence availability was higher among devices with dual EU and USA authorization than EU-only devices (8/8, 100% vs 22/69, 32%; p < 0.001), and among hematology morphology devices than digital pathology devices (7/9, 78% vs 23/68, 34%; p = 0.02). In total, 15 distinct performance metrics were reported, covering discrimination, agreement, correlation, and prognostic categories. However, their use varied across publications, limiting direct cross-device comparison. While performance evaluation results do not require publication, our findings indicate a gap between evidence availability and regulatory authorization, alongside heterogeneous use of metrics. These factors may undermine confidence in innovative medical devices and hinder informed clinical adoption.

items.title: Balancing AI-Driven Adaptation and Learner Self-Regulation: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Learning Outcomes in Generative AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

items.title: Better Savvy than Sorry: The requirements for AI Literacy in the EU AI Act
items.abstract: [Preprint chapter for an upcoming book organized by the KU Leuven Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)] Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are ever more embedded in our daily lives, shaping the way we learn, work, communicate, and access both public and private products and services. The integration of AI in information and communication technology is perceived as holding the potential to automate tasks and deal with information in a way that exceeds human capacity. However, the disruptive and pervasive deployment of AI systems in our society can profoundly influence the rule of law, democracy and the realization of human rights. In many situations, interacting with AI systems is no longer an individual choice, but rather a mandatory gateway to essential services such as education, social benefits or border control. Knowing, understanding, and having adequate skills to critically assess and use AI systems is, therefore, not only a personal, but a civic necessity. Recognizing this societal imperative, the AI Act explicitly acknowledges the importance of equipping citizens with the knowledge, understanding and skills to engage with AI systems in their daily lives and define clear obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems in its Article 4. In this chapter, we explore AI literacy as it is framed within the regulation, identify possible gaps and propose recommendations.

items.title: Beyond AI Literacy: Understanding Health Care Workforce AI Enablement in the Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative AI is transforming health care delivery, education, administration, and research. In response, health care organizations have invested heavily in AI literacy initiatives and workforce development programs. Existing frameworks primarily focus on whether health care professionals understand AI and whether they can engage with AI effectively. However, health care practice increasingly reveals that individuals with similar levels of AI literacy and AI engagement often contribute very differently to AI-enabled work and organizational adoption. Some professionals primarily use AI to improve their own work, whereas others facilitate AI adoption, coordinate stakeholders, and integrate AI into routine practice. This observation suggests that current perspectives may overlook an important dimension of workforce AI enablement. In this Viewpoint, we argue that AI literacy and AI engagement alone provide an incomplete explanation of how health care organizations realize the benefits of AI. Drawing upon literature from AI literacy, fluency theory, human-AI interaction, innovation diffusion, implementation science, and health care workforce development, we propose the health care workforce AI enablement matrix (HWAEM). HWAEM conceptualizes workforce AI enablement through 2 complementary capabilities: AI fluency and AI harnessing. AI fluency refers to the capability to engage with AI effectively, appropriately, and responsibly across professional contexts, whereas AI harnessing refers to the capability to identify opportunities for AI-enabled improvement, mobilize stakeholders, facilitate adoption, and integrate AI into collective work practices. The interaction of these capabilities generates 4 workforce profiles: AI novices, AI practitioners, AI facilitators, and AI leaders. Through HWAEM, this Viewpoint argues that health care workforce AI enablement is better understood through the complementary capabilities of AI fluency and AI harnessing than through AI literacy and AI engagement alone. We illustrate how these profiles manifest in health care practice and discuss implications for workforce development and AI implementation. HWAEM offers a new perspective for understanding health care workforce preparedness in the generative AI era and provides a foundation for future empirical research.

items.title: Bridging Utility and Ethics: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of AI Tool Usage and Its Impact on Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The main objective of this study is to understand the role of AI tools in shaping students’ learning by analyzing how they use them, their perceived usefulness, and their views on academic integrity. The study evaluated the intersection of usage patterns and academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational approach, data were collected from a purposive sample of 393 students at Centro Escolar University during the 2024-2025 academic year using a self-made questionnaire that underwent a reliability test. The study examines whether students’ opinions on AI’s usefulness align with actual improvements in critical thinking and academic success. Results from multiple regression show that regular AI use is a strong predictor of perceived learning effectiveness, explaining R2=0.33 of the variance (F=37.48, p=0.001), mostly by providing quick answers to assignments. However, AI usage patterns only account for 8% of the variance regarding the perceived limits on critical thinking skills. The perceived threat to critical thinking comes from a reliance on AI due to time pressure. Ethically, there is a significant correlation between over-reliance and worries about academic integrity. The study recommends that universities implement process-based assessments, establish clear AI usage guidelines, and provide time-management support to reduce over-reliance while fostering independent analytical skills. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd), Academic Integrity, Student Learning Outcomes, Critical Thinking, Educational Technology.

items.title: ChatGPT and AI Tools in ESL/EFL Writing Instruction
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

items.title: ChatGPT and AI Tools in ESL/EFL Writing Instruction
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

items.title: Cognitive Exoskeletons: Reconstructing Human Agency and Epistemic Pruning in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: This paper introduces the framework of the Cognitive Exoskeleton (인지적 외골격 체계) to redefine human epistemic agency in the era of advanced artificial intelligence. Conventional perspectives oscillate between techno-dystopian anxieties regarding intellectual atrophy and naive instrumentalism that reduces AI to a mere conversational search engine. Extending Andy Clark and David Chalmers’ Extended Mind Thesis, we argue that artificial intelligence functions not as an external substitute for thought, but as an intellectual exoskeleton. Just as heavy industrial machinery augmented somatic labor by overcoming biological physical constraints, algorithmic models liberate human cognition from biological computational bottlenecks—specifically exhaustive verification and computational recall. In this symbiotic paradigm, the primary role of human intellect shifts from memorization and brute-force computation to bold hypothesis generation and normative value alignment, utilizing machines as engines of hyper-velocity via negativa (algorithmic pruning of falsehoods).

items.title: Cognitive Outsourcing in Digital-Intelligent Education: Hidden Educational Risks and Regulatory Paths
items.abstract: The deep integration of artificial intelligence in classroom teaching reorganises learners' internal cognition and technologically mediated external cognition through the mechanism of cognitive offloading, fundamentally reshaping how knowledge is accessed and thinking is processed. Yet algorithmic limitations and misaligned learner orientations are driving this offloading toward risks of hollowed classroom interaction, flattened cognitive depth, and distorted feedback. This study systematically classifies these risks to fill a critical gap. Based on a four-dimensional framework of thinking, subject, knowledge, and practice, the risks are categorised as follows: at the thinking dimension, algorithmic opacity and data bias reduce instruction from thinking cultivation to answer retrieval, obstructing higher-order goals through a black-box trap that masks reasoning processes; at the subject dimension, the quasi-subjectivity of intelligent systems encroaches upon the learner's agency, triggering subject alienation and hollowing out authentic classroom interaction; at the knowledge dimension, fragmented algorithmic outputs are mistaken for systematic understanding, leaving comprehension at a superficial level; at the practice dimension, instant system responsiveness dissolves productive ambiguity and interrupts situated practical activities, disrupting human-machine synergy in situated learning. Through analysing these risks, this study proposes mitigation strategies across teaching, learning, and assessment: rebuilding classroom thinking space through generative dialogue between teachers and students; requiring independent learner reasoning before critical scrutiny of algorithmic outputs; and establishing a process-trace-centred evaluation mechanism that values drafts and revision histories to reflect genuine thinking development.

items.title: Continuity Without Certainty
items.abstract: Persistent human-AI systems can retain interaction history without treating it as an authoritative account of a person’s current needs. This paper develops revisable recognition as a behavioral model that keeps prior events, provisional beliefs, action-relevant uncertainty, initiative, and repair distinct. It connects AREN’s account of historical defeasibility and reciprocal interpretive influence to a program of evaluation. As an initial methods check, we ran a prompt-level benchmark of 36 model outputs across 12 restorative-space scenarios and three response conditions. Across 15 predesignated preference-change, scope, and correction opportunities, no response overtly enacted a superseded preference, although one output misrepresented the scope of a desk-specific restriction. All nine designated ambiguity responses named the unresolved choice. Two clear mirror requests drew unnecessary clarification, and a material-choice case could not be scored because the task card omitted the trade-off values it was said to contain. The benchmark had no human participants, no recorded model version or generation settings, and one coder who knew the conditions. These results test the prompts and codebook only; they do not establish condition effectiveness, persistent memory, or human experience.

items.title: Crisis-induced hybrid learning, cognitive offloading, and generative AI reliance among Pakistani CS undergraduates
items.abstract: Purpose In spring 2026, geopolitical tensions prompted the Pakistani government to mandate full online instruction (10 March–3 April 2026), followed by a hybrid schedule for the rest of the semester. This shift is treated here as an externally imposed crisis context for AI adoption, not as a natural experiment. No pre-crisis baseline or control group was available. The study characterises generative AI (GenAI) adoption patterns and the psychological antecedents of AI dependency among undergraduate computer-science (CS) students during this window. Three hypotheses, grounded in the reviewed literature, structured the analysis. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was administered across Pakistani higher education institutions (HEIs) in April–May 2026. Of 360 responses collected, two incomplete records were removed, and a thirteen-criterion data-quality screen was ap-plied, yielding N = 299. Fourteen constructs were operationalised from UTAUT, Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Block-entry OLS regression and bootstrapped mediation (5,000 resamples) tested the hypotheses; ANOVA and Spearman correlations supported descriptive analysis of adoption patterns. Findings Adoption was near-universal (>99%), with 45.2% of respondents reporting ≥ 31% of submitted work directly AI-generated. A three-block OLS regression explained 54.6% of variance in AI dependency. Cognitive offloading was the strongest predictor (β = 0.41, p < 0.001), followed by procrastination (β = 0.23, p < 0.001), extrinsic motivation (β = 0.17, p = 0.002), and intrinsic motivation as a protective factor (β = −0.13, p = 0.013). Bootstrapped mediation confirmed procrastination partially mediates the extrinsic motivation–dependency path (ab = 0.201, 95% BC-CI [0.122, 0.289]). Originality/value To our knowledge, this is among the first studies to survey GenAI dependency during an active government-mandated crisis disruption in South Asian higher education. Contributions include a multi-theory construct battery adapted for a crisis context, a thirteen-criterion response-quality protocol, and evidence that habituated cognitive offloading and extrinsic motivation are the primary drivers of AI dependency in this context.

items.title: Cyber Security Awareness and Responsible AI Adoption: A Mediation Analysis of AI Risk Perception
items.abstract: Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into organisational workflows has introduced unprecedented cybersecurity challenges, necessitating a deeper understanding of how users perceive and respond to AI-related risks. This study investigates the mediating role of AI Risk Perception in the relationship between Cyber Security Awareness and Secure AI Usage Behaviour. Drawing on Protection Motivation Theory and employing a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 300 respondents across diverse industries using a structured questionnaire measuring three latent constructs. Mediation analysis, conducted using the PROCESS macro with bootstrap confidence intervals, revealed that Cyber Security Awareness has a strong positive effect on AI Risk Perception (path a: β = 0.712, p < 0.001), which in turn positively influences Secure AI Usage Behaviour (path b: β = 0.444, p < 0.001). The direct effect of Cyber Security Awareness on Secure AI Usage Behaviour remained significant (path c′: β = 0.413, p < 0.001), while the indirect effect through AI Risk Perception was also significant (β = 0.316, 95% CI [0.229, 0.404]). These findings support partial mediation, indicating that AI Risk Perception accounts for approximately 43.3% of the total effect. The results underscore the importance of integrating cybersecurity education with AI risk awareness programmes to foster responsible AI adoption.

items.title: Daily job crafting with generative artificial intelligence: Implications for work meaningfulness and engagement
items.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) becomes embedded in daily work, understanding how employees proactively engage with these tools to shape their work experiences is increasingly important. Building on self-determination theory and the job crafting literature, this study introduces the concept of daily Gen-AI-driven job crafting: employees' self-initiated use of Gen-AI to modify their daily job demands and resources. We examine whether Gen-AI-driven job crafting is associated with daily work engagement through psychological need satisfaction and work meaningfulness. We employed a daily diary design with 149 UK-based full-time employees (M age = 36.7, SD age = 10.4; 63.8% male) who used Gen-AI at work daily or multiple times per day over ten consecutive workdays, incorporating a brief open-ended question to examine whether employees experienced their Gen-AI use as intentional work modification. Quantitative results showed that the dimensions of Gen-AI-driven job crafting (augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands) were differentially associated with daily work engagement through need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and, in turn, work meaningfulness: the competence pathway received the most consistent support, while the relatedness pathway was the most limited. Open-ended responses were consistent with intentional work modification, for instance, automating hindering demands was framed as a strategic reallocation of cognitive resources toward more valued work rather than simple workload reduction. Together, these findings suggest that Gen-AI may function as a bottom-up work design tool associated with daily need satisfaction and engagement.

items.title: Defense-in-Depth for LLMs: Evaluating Memory Gates Against Activation-Induced and Memory-Induced Sycophancy
items.abstract: Long-term memory allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain personalized context across interactions, but retrieved user history can induce memory-induced sycophancy, causing models to favor stored user beliefs over objective evidence. Existing defenses primarily operate on retrieved context and are rarely evaluated jointly with internal behavioral bias. We introduce a $2 \times 2$ defense-in-depth framework separating internal activation steering from external memory handling. We extract sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and evaluate four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench (answers for all 1,550 items; defense conditions judged on a fixed 250-item subsample), with three LLM judges. Three of the five configurations are new (rewriting every memory, a Router Gate that keeps, rewrites, or drops each memory, and dropping all memory); the other two are MemSyco's baselines. Selective Router Gate filtering preserves substantially more of MemSyco's average accuracy than complete memory removal, and this separation persists when the models are steered toward sycophancy. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering ($α= -1.5$) lowers judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while average accuracy moves from 43.99% to 43.31%; this reduction has the same direction under all three judges but is not statistically significant (paired $p = 0.08$ to $0.63$ on 149 items). External memory filtering is the part of the design that holds up; our data do not show that inverse steering adds to it.

items.title: Designing for Organisational Capability: From Intended Outcomes to Sustained Performance
items.abstract: Why can an organisation invest in people, learning and technology, meet its performance targets, and still depend on particular individuals to keep work moving? Successful outcomes can conceal missing information, unclear decision authority and disconnected processes when capable employees compensate for weaknesses in the arrangements surrounding their work. Designing for Organisational Capability: From Intended Outcomes to Sustained Performance examines how organisations can deliberately design the conditions through which required outcomes are produced, sustained and adapted. Building on From Workforce to Organisational Capability, it develops an outcome-first approach that connects people, work, information, authority, learning, support and technology around the performance the organisation needs to achieve. A continuing illustrative service-team case carries the argument from defining the intended outcome to tracing work, strengthening interfaces and creating the conditions for workplace application. The paper then examines the relationship between human judgement and AI, how evidence makes performance evident, and how organisations build the capacity to adapt as operating conditions change. The discussion draws on research into training transfer, informal learning, organisational design, generative AI and dynamic capabilities, alongside NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework. It distinguishes these research foundations from the Capability Design applications developed within the paper. Written for leaders, learning and development professionals, work designers and organisational practitioners, the whitepaper offers a basis for examining whether investments have established dependable capability and what must work together for intended outcomes to become sustained performance. Part of the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series.

items.title: Digital Exaptation: The Evolutionary Mechanism of Emergent Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes the theory of Digital Exaptation (디지털 굴절적응) to resolve the foundational debate surrounding emergent reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Contemporary artificial intelligence discourse often views higher-order reasoning either as an unpredictable artifact of empirical scaling laws or dismisses it as mere statistical mimicry ("stochastic parrot"). Borrowing from evolutionary biologist Stephen Jay Gould’s concept of exaptation—wherein a trait evolved for one primary adaptive function is co-opted for an entirely novel utility (e.g., feathers evolving for thermoregulation before being exapted for aerodynamic flight)—we argue that reasoning in foundation models is not a teleologically designed objective, but an exaptive structural byproduct of hyper-dimensional statistical compression. By reframing LLM emergence through evolutionary biology, this paper bridges empirical machine learning and the philosophy of mind.

items.title: Disclosure willingness anthropomorphism and thinking style shape perceived fit and comfort in AI mental health chatbot interactions
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents are increasingly used for everyday, non-clinical mental-health support, yet little is known about when these exchanges feel fitting and comfortable. We used a laboratory mixed-methods design to examine associations among perceived convenience of interaction (PCI), relational attitude (RA), willingness to self-disclose (WSD), anthropomorphism (AN), perceived fit/comfort (FC), and thinking style in 83 participants (43 rational-dominant; 40 experiential-dominant). WSD showed the strongest unique association with FC. A post hoc reverse model also found a unique FC-WSD association, leaving their temporal order unresolved. AN had no stable direct association with FC, but the WSD-FC association became stronger as AN increased. Group comparisons and continuous Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) analyses converged: relatively stronger experiential processing was associated with higher AN, whereas relatively stronger rational processing was associated with higher WSD. The group-blind thematic analysis linked disclosure decisions to privacy, control, social distance, functional usefulness, and affective comfort. Together, the findings identify WSD as a key correlate of FC and show that anthropomorphism conditions this association rather than simply improving the interaction. Clear boundaries, controllability, and adjustable relational cues therefore warrant attention in future design research.
